newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany and France seek more policy coordination.
newsitem.headline: Germany and France seek more policy coordination.

text.p: Germany and France, the motors of Europe's integration drive, are seeking ways to improve their own policy coordination to present a more united front in foreign affairs, a spokesman said on Monday.

The two countries have worked out proposals for closer consultation on the main issues, joint trips abroad by their foreign ministers and more personnel swaps between German and French ministries, foreign ministry spokesman Martin Erdmann said.
The suggestions are still at the planning stage and will not be on the agenda when Chancellor Helmut Kohl and President Jacques Chirac meet over dinner in Bonn on Wednesday, he added.
Erdmann said the proposals were meant to push further the bilateral cooperation Bonn and Paris have pursued since their post-war reconciliation embodied in the Elysee Treaty of 1963.
"We're not trying to invent new wheels for the tandem, just improve the pedals we already have," he told Reuters.

Bonn and Paris have been trying to improve coordination ever since Chirac upset the balance with surprise announcements like his resumption of nuclear testing or the abolition of French military conscription.

There have also been tensions over defence issues, where budget constraints have cast doubt over some joint weapons projects and French initiatives -- such as the call for a European to head NATO's southern command -- have made the more pro-U.S. leaders in Bonn differ with Washington.

The two countries approved a new defence pact last December that declares their security interests inseparable, declares support for NATO and agrees to discuss the role of France's nuclear forces in a common European defence.

Under the new proposals, worked out by the policy planning staffs of both foreign ministries, senior officials should make much more detailed preparations for the regular six-monthly bilateral consultations between Kohl and Chirac. Each side would pledge to involve the other in all important decisions.
The two countries should identify long-term policy goals both could work on and send their foreign ministers on joint trips, especially to the U.S., to underline their common stand.
They should aim to take more joint stands in NATO, the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) and the United Nations, the paper suggested.
There should also be more staff swaps, both at the foreign ministry and at other ministries which have to cooperate on the European level, to further integrate policy making, it added.
The German foreign ministry has diplomats from allied countries like France, Britain and the U.S. working as part of its staff, but there are usually only one or two per country.
Bonn and Paris tried to open a joint embassy in Mongolia in the early 1990s but France's constitutional court ruled this violated French law.

Erdmann said the European Union's inter-governmental conference (IGC), which is due this June to approve reforms to the way the EU works, would create a common foreign and security policy that will affect the German-French partnership.
"We want to improve German-French cooperation in these areas that will be affected by the common foreign and security policy," he said.
